osint.name: Epieos
osint.summary: Reverse-look up an email or phone number to find linked Google, LinkedIn and other accounts. Freemium web app, no install for basic lookups.
osint.overview:
Epieos is a web-based reverse lookup for email addresses and phone numbers. Paste an identifier and it returns linked Google account details, connected services and public traces — without notifying the target and without logging your query. Basic lookups are free; deeper modules covering LinkedIn, Facebook, fitness apps and more need a paid plan.

It is the fastest option when you want answers in a browser instead of a terminal: no install, no syntax, just paste and read. Because results come from live service responses rather than a stale database, re-running a lookup over time can surface newly linked accounts.
osint.key_features:
• Reverse lookup for both email addresses and phone numbers
  • Surfaces linked Google account details and connected services
  • No query logging and no notification to the target
  • No install — guided web workflow for beginners
  • Paid modules unlock LinkedIn, Facebook, fitness apps and more
  • Used by investigators, journalists and enterprises
osint.install_guide:
No installation needed: it runs in your browser.

  1. Open Epieos below and choose Email or Phone lookup.
  2. Enter the address or number and confirm the terms.
  3. Review linked accounts, then pivot on each finding elsewhere.

Free tier covers basic lookups; advanced modules need a paid plan (check Pricing on their site).
osint.use_case:
A rental listing asks for a deposit over email, and the price feels too good. Paste the lister's address into Epieos. Within a minute you see linked Google reviews, a Skype handle and other connected traces — or a complete blank. Read them for consistency: reviews spanning years under one name build confidence, while mismatched names and fresh accounts are classic scam markers.

Never send money on email evidence alone. Use the lookup as a filter — consistent history earns a video viewing, inconsistency ends the conversation.
osint.faqs:
Is Epieos free?

Basic lookups are free. Deeper modules covering networks like LinkedIn and Facebook need a paid plan — check the Pricing page on their site for current rates.

What can it look up?

Email to Google account, to LinkedIn and other linked services; phone numbers; and public breach references. Each module returns whatever that service exposes.

Do lookups notify the target?

The free modules query public endpoints, not the person. Even so, investigate only people you have a legitimate reason to look into.

Does it store my queries?

Epieos requires an account for most modules and keeps a query history, so treat your searches as logged. Use a work account for client work.

osint.name: ExifTool
osint.summary: Read, write and strip EXIF and other metadata from photos, video, PDFs and Office files. The de-facto standard, free, on every OS.
osint.overview:
ExifTool by Phil Harvey is the reference tool for file metadata. Point it at a photo and it reveals camera model, GPS coordinates, timestamps, software history and hundreds of other embedded fields — the raw material of image verification work.

Journalists use it to check whether a viral photo is really from where it claims; investigators use it to place a device at a location and time; privacy-conscious users run it in reverse, stripping metadata before sharing. It reads and writes metadata across a huge range of formats, and almost every other metadata tool is built on top of it.
osint.key_features:
• Reads metadata from images, video, audio, PDF and documents
  • Reveals GPS, camera, timestamps and editing history
  • Writes and strips metadata for safe sharing
  • Scriptable CLI trusted in forensic workflows
  • Single dependency-free install on every major OS
  • Free and open source
osint.install_guide:
# Debian / Ubuntu / Kali

sudo apt install libimage-exiftool-perl



## macOS

brew install exiftool



# Read all metadata from a photo

exiftool photo.jpg



## GPS coordinates only

exiftool -gpslatitude -gpslongitude photo.jpg



# Strip all metadata (safe sharing)

exiftool -all= photo.jpg
osint.use_case:
A dramatic photo spreads online claiming to show last night's protest in your city. Save a copy and run ExifTool on it. The timestamps and any GPS data tell you when and where the camera actually was — if the metadata says noon three years ago in another country, the claim collapses without any further debate.

Flip the workflow for your own photos: run ExifTool with the strip-all flag before posting, so your location and device details never travel with the image.
osint.faqs:
Is ExifTool free?

Yes. ExifTool is free and open source.

What metadata actually survives today?

Cameras and scanners still embed rich EXIF; most social networks strip it on upload. GPS coordinates, device model and timestamps are the usual finds.

How do I strip metadata before publishing?

exiftool -all= file.jpg removes everything; -overwrite_original writes in place. Keep a copy of the original if it is evidence.

Can it read more than photos?

Yes: PDF documents, Office properties, video containers, and even file-system timestamps with care. It is the general metadata reader.

osint.name: Holehe
osint.summary: Check whether an email is registered on 120+ sites — Instagram, Spotify, Adobe and more — from the command line. Free and open source.
osint.overview:
Holehe answers one question fast: is this email address signed up on a given site? It tests the address against more than 120 platforms — Reddit, GitHub, Discord, Spotify, Amazon and many more — using each site's own password-reset and registration flows, without sending anything to the address owner.

The result is a clean registered-or-not list that is perfect for pivoting from an email to a set of accounts: every "registered" hit is a new place to look. Investigators pair it with username tools to connect an address to handles, and defenders use it to audit which services a corporate domain is scattered across.
osint.key_features:
• 120+ platforms: Reddit, GitHub, Discord, Spotify, Amazon and more
  • Uses official reset and registration flows — no intrusive probing
  • Clean registered-or-not verdict per site
  • CSV export for case files
  • Fast async engine — one command per email
  • Free and open source (MIT)
osint.install_guide:
# Install with pip (Python 3.9+)

pip install holehe



# Check an email address

holehe test@example.com



## Save results to a CSV file

holehe test@example.com --csv
osint.use_case:
During incident response you learn an employee's address appeared in a breach dump. Before forcing company-wide resets, scope the exposure: run the address through Holehe and list every platform where it is registered. That list becomes your reset checklist — start with email, cloud storage and code hosting, then work down.

Document each confirmed account for the incident report. Anything Holehe flags that the employee does not recognize may indicate an account created with a leaked password elsewhere, which is exactly how credential-stuffing chains begin.
osint.faqs:
Is Holehe free?

Yes. Holehe is free and open source under the MIT license.

What does 'registered' mean?

The service's password-reset or signup endpoint responded in a way that implies the account exists. It is an inference, not a confirmation.

Why are some sites always wrong?

Endpoints that answer identically for known and unknown emails produce false positives. Cross-check any hit on the site itself.

Is it rate limited?

Different sites throttle differently. Use --only-used to cut noise and expect some sites to block you after repeated runs.

osint.name: Maigret
osint.summary: Username search across 3,000+ sites with HTML, PDF or JSON reports plus leaked-data checks. Free, open source, command line.
osint.overview:
Maigret collects information about a username across more than 3000 websites and known data leaks. Where Sherlock answers "does this profile exist?", Maigret goes further: it pulls public profile details such as linked IDs, accounts and interests, and compiles everything into structured HTML and PDF reports you can hand to a client or file with a case.

It is the better pick when one username needs a full written report rather than a quick existence check — fraud reviews, due-diligence screening and long-running person investigations. Like every OSINT tool, its output is leads, not proof: open the linked profiles and corroborate the interesting hits before acting on them.
osint.key_features:
• 3000+ sites plus username checks against known data leaks
  • Auto-generated HTML and PDF investigation reports
  • Extracts linked IDs, accounts and interests from public profiles
  • Cookie-based authenticated checks for logged-in sources
  • Fingerprint database kept current by the community
  • Free and open source, CLI-first with Docker support
osint.install_guide:
# Recommended: isolated install with pipx (Python 3.9+)

pipx install maigret



# Check a username and open the HTML report

maigret user123 --html



# Also generate a PDF report

maigret user123 --html --pdf
osint.use_case:
You are hiring a freelance developer whose proposal links a username but no portfolio. Run Maigret on the handle with HTML output and read the report like a CV: old StackOverflow answers reveal real skill history, forum posts show communication style, and any leak-database hit tells you to ask about password habits before granting repository access.

Verify the two most relevant profiles by opening them directly. If the timeline and skills match the proposal, proceed to a paid trial task. If the username barely exists outside the proposal itself, treat the application with caution.
osint.faqs:
Maigret or Sherlock — which should I use?

Use Sherlock for a fast existence check across 400+ sites. Use Maigret when you need depth: 3000+ sites, leaked-data checks and a written HTML or PDF report.

How many sites does it check?

Around 3,000, ordered by popularity, so -top-sites 500 gives a fast first pass and the full run is the exhaustive one.

What reports can it make?

HTML, PDF and JSON dossiers (--html, -P, --json). The HTML report keeps the found-profile links, which is what you actually cite.

Do I need API keys?

No. The default checks are free; a few optional modules that read leaked-data sources need their own keys.

osint.name: PhoneInfoga
osint.summary: Look up a phone number's carrier, country, line type and public mentions. Free, open source, with a CLI and a REST API.
osint.overview:
PhoneInfoga is an open-source phone number investigator. Enter a number in international format and it reports the carrier and country, checks the number against data-leak databases, and searches for public mentions and linked messenger accounts.

Version 2 runs as a local web server, so beginners never have to leave the browser while advanced users keep the terminal workflow. The one-command Docker deployment removes the usual dependency pain, which makes it practical for scam triage desks and fraud teams that need answers in minutes, not setup hours.
osint.key_features:
• Carrier, country and line-type detection from any number
  • Checks leaks and public mentions of the number
  • Local web UI plus the classic terminal workflow
  • One-command Docker deployment — no dependency hell
  • Number reputation signals for scam and spam triage
  • Free and open source (GPL-3.0)
osint.install_guide:
# Easiest: run with Docker

docker pull sundowndev/phoneinfoga:latest

docker run -it -p 5000:5000 sundowndev/phoneinfoga serve --port=5000



# Then open http://localhost:5000 in your browser,

# or scan directly from the terminal:

docker run -it sundowndev/phoneinfoga scan -n +33612345678
osint.use_case:
A text message claims your parcel is held and links a "redelivery" page asking for card details. Copy the sender number into PhoneInfoga in international format. The scan returns the real carrier and country plus any leak or mention history — compare that with the story: a domestic parcel service texting from a foreign prepaid range is a failed check.

Screenshot the result, block the number and report the message as smishing. If the number shows prior scam reports, include them in the report so the pattern is visible.
osint.faqs:
What format does the number need?

International format with the country code, for example +33612345678.

Can I find the owner of a number?

No tool can. PhoneInfoga aggregates public signals: carrier, line type, country and any footprint the number left in search results.

Why does the carrier look wrong?

Number portability. A prefix shows the original allocation; the current carrier needs a live HLR lookup, which most free tiers do not provide.

Do I need API keys?

Not for the built-in scanners. numverify and similar improve coverage but are optional, and the CLI runs without them.

osint.name: Sherlock
osint.summary: Hunt down a username across 400+ social networks and websites. Free, open-source, runs on your machine.
osint.overview:
Sherlock is one of the most popular open-source username investigation tools. Give it a username and it checks that handle across more than 400 social networks and websites — GitHub, Instagram, Reddit, Telegram, TikTok and hundreds more — then saves every hit to a text file for that username. Results link straight to the matching profile so you can verify each one by hand.

Journalists use it to verify whether a source's handle is real, security teams use it to spot executive impersonation, and hiring managers use it for lightweight background checks. It is a lookup tool, not a hacking tool: it only visits public profile pages and reports which ones exist, and every finding should still be opened and confirmed manually.

Power users get structured exports (CSV, XLSX, JSON), Tor and proxy support for sensitive cases, and a community-maintained site list that can be extended with custom targets.
osint.key_features:
• Checks 400+ social networks and websites from a single command
  • Saves every hit to a per-username text file with direct profile links
  • CSV, XLSX and JSON export for reports and further analysis
  • Tor and proxy support for sensitive investigations
  • Site list is community-maintained JSON — add your own targets
  • Free and open source (MIT), runs fully on your machine
osint.install_guide:
# Recommended: isolated install with pipx (Python 3.9+)

pipx install sherlock-project



# Check a single username

sherlock user123



# Check several usernames at once

sherlock user1 user2 user3
osint.use_case:
A marketplace seller contacts you on Telegram with a great price and a username that also appears as their "shop name". Before sending any money, run that handle through Sherlock. In a few minutes you get a list of everywhere the name exists: perhaps a matching Instagram with three years of posts and a GitHub with real commits — or perhaps nothing at all outside Telegram, which is itself an answer.

Open the two or three strongest hits. Compare avatars, writing style and account ages. If the Instagram joined last week and the photos look stock, walk away. If everything lines up across years, you have done in ten minutes what used to take an afternoon of manual searching.
osint.faqs:
Is Sherlock free?

Yes. Sherlock is free and open source under the MIT license. It runs entirely on your own machine, needs no account and no API key.

How many sites does it cover?

400+ popular platforms, ordered by traffic. --site lets you check a single site, and the data file is easy to extend.

Are the results reliable?

A hit means the username resolved on that site, not that it is the same person. Two matching identifiers are still the minimum to link accounts.

Why so many false positives?

Sites with soft-404 responses return 200 for any username. Use --print-found with --timeout, and verify unusual hits by hand.

osint.name: Shodan
osint.summary: The search engine for internet-connected devices, services and exposures. Freemium web app plus API.
osint.overview:
Shodan continuously scans the internet and indexes banners from servers, routers, webcams, databases and industrial systems. Instead of searching web pages, you search devices: find open ports, outdated software, exposed databases and misconfigured services by IP, hostname, port or organisation.

Defenders use it to discover their own forgotten exposures — the unpatched camera, the database without a password, the test server that was never taken down. A free account covers basic lookups; serious use with API access, historical data and network monitoring is paid. Every result includes the raw banner, so findings can be verified rather than taken on faith.
osint.key_features:
• Searchable index of banners from millions of devices
  • Filters by port, country, organisation, product and vulnerability
  • Exposes misconfigurations: open databases, default credentials, outdated builds
  • REST API, CLI and integrations with Maltego, Nmap and Metasploit
  • Monitoring and alerts for your own attack surface on paid plans
  • Free tier for basic lookups; membership unlocks history and API credits
osint.install_guide:
No installation needed for the web version.

  1. Create a free account on Shodan below.
  2. Try a starter query such as port:22 or an IP address.
  3. Open a result to see open ports, banners and known vulnerabilities.

For automation, install the CLI (pip install shodan) and add your API key with: shodan init YOUR_API_KEY.
osint.use_case:
Ask your network team for the company's public IP ranges, then search them on Shodan. You are looking for surprises: a printer admin page with default credentials, an old camera feed, a database port answering the whole internet, a test server someone forgot in 2021.

Each surprise becomes a ticket: restrict the port, patch the service, or take the host down. Re-run the same search quarterly — exposure drifts, and Shodan notices new devices before internal inventories do.
osint.faqs:
Is Shodan free?

A free account covers basic lookups. Membership and API credits for automation, history and monitoring are paid.

Where does the data come from?

Shodan scans the internet continuously and indexes service banners. It shows you what was visible at scan time, not necessarily now.

Is using Shodan active scanning?

No - you are reading someone else's scan results, which keeps you passive. Verifying a hit against the host is what turns it active.

How do filters help?

org:, country:, product: and port: narrow the index to what matters. The free tier has limited filters and no historical data.

osint.name: SpiderFoot
osint.summary: Automate OSINT collection across 200+ modules from one web UI or CLI, with a correlator that links findings into a graph. Free and open source.
osint.overview:
SpiderFoot is an open-source OSINT automation platform. Instead of running ten tools by hand, you give SpiderFoot one target — a domain, IP, email, username or ASN — and its 200+ modules query threat feeds, search engines, DNS records, breach data and social sources automatically, then correlate everything into a single browsable report.

It runs as a local web app with a command-line option for scripting, and because it is self-hosted your targets never leave your infrastructure. Teams schedule recurring scans to watch their own exposure drift over time; investigators use one-off scans to turn a single identifier into a full entity graph in minutes.
osint.key_features:
• 200+ modules: feeds, DNS, breaches, search, social, threat intel
  • One target in — correlated graph and browsable report out
  • Self-hosted: your targets never leave your infrastructure
  • Scheduled and API-driven scans for continuous monitoring
  • Built-in visualizations of entity relationships
  • Free and open source (MIT)
osint.install_guide:
# Clone and install (Python 3.9+)

git clone https://github.com/smicallef/spiderfoot.git

cd spiderfoot

pip install -r requirements.txt



## Start the web interface

python3 ./sf.py -l 127.0.0.1:5001



# Open http://127.0.0.1:5001, create a new scan,

# enter your target and pick the modules to run.
osint.use_case:
All you have is a suspicious domain from a phishing email. Create a SpiderFoot scan with that domain as the seed and let its modules work: DNS records, certificate logs, breach data, threat feeds and similar-domain searches run automatically and link into one graph.

Read the graph outward from the seed. A cluster of lookalike domains registered the same week through the same registrar is a campaign, not a coincidence — export the report and hand the indicator list to your blocking and takedown process.
osint.faqs:
Is SpiderFoot fully passive?

Behavior depends on enabled modules and data sources; review module behavior before a run.

How many modules does it have?

Over 200, split into passive (third-party data) and active (direct to target) sets. Passive modules need no API key; the key-based ones add depth.

What is the correlator for?

It cross-links findings from different modules, which is how a domain turns into an organisation, then into contacts. Without it, you just get rows.

Can I run a scan from the CLI?

Yes: sf.py -s example.com -t DOMAIN_NAME -m all -o tab. Useful for scheduled recon; the UI is for exploring results.

osint.name: theHarvester
osint.summary: Gather emails, subdomains, hosts and employee names for a domain from 20+ public sources. Free, open source, command line.
osint.overview:
theHarvester is a classic reconnaissance tool for the early stages of an investigation. Give it a domain name and it passively collects emails, subdomains, hostnames, IP addresses and employee names from public sources — search engines, certificate transparency logs, DNS dumps and more.

Security teams run it against their own organisation to map what is exposed before attackers do; investigators run it to expand one domain into a full target list of people, hosts and addresses. Everything it gathers is already public — the skill is in querying broadly and correlating the results, which is exactly what the tool automates.
osint.key_features:
• Emails, subdomains, hosts, IPs and employee names per domain
  • Passive sources: certificate transparency, DNS dumps, search engines
  • XML and JSON output for piping into other tooling
  • Screenshot and takeover checks for discovered subdomains
  • A standard first step in pentest and red-team recon
  • Free and open source (GPL)
osint.install_guide:
# Clone and install (Python 3.9+)

git clone https://github.com/laramies/theHarvester.git

cd theHarvester

pip install -r requirements.txt



## Basic run against a domain

python3 theHarvester.py -d example.com -b all



## Limit sources and save output

python3 theHarvester.py -d example.com -b crtsh,hackertarget -f results
osint.use_case:
You have just been authorized to test a company's public exposure. Start with theHarvester against their main domain: within minutes you hold a list of employee emails, subdomains and hostnames — the exact raw material an attacker would collect first.

Hand the subdomain list to your DNS checks and the email list to a breach lookup. Every forgotten staging host or exposed webmail login you find becomes a finding in the report, with the remediation advice to inventory subdomains and enforce multi-factor authentication on everything public.
osint.faqs:
Is every result accurate?

No. Sources may be incomplete or stale, so validate findings before reporting them.

Which sources need API keys?

crtsh, certspotter, otx, rapiddns and urlscan need none. Shodan, Hunter, SecurityTrails and similar read keys from api-keys.yaml.

Why does Google return nothing?

Google blocks automated queries quickly. Use bing, duckduckgo or crtsh instead, and keep -l modest.

Is this active scanning?

No - it queries third-party indexes and public sources. Nothing is sent to the target, which is why it is safe at the recon stage.

osint.name: WhatsMyName
osint.summary: Check a username across hundreds of sites instantly in your browser. Free web app, nothing to install.
osint.overview:
WhatsMyName is a browser-based username checker maintained by the WebBreacher project. Type a username and it tests it against hundreds of websites in seconds, showing found profiles as clickable links. Because it runs entirely as a web page there is nothing to install and no command line needed — the best first tool for beginners.

Experienced investigators use it as a triage step before heavier tools: a 30-second WhatsMyName run tells you whether a handle is worth a full Sherlock or Maigret pass. The underlying site list is downloadable, so the same checks can run offline or inside your own scripts.
osint.key_features:
• Zero install — runs as a single web page
  • Hundreds of sites checked in seconds with clickable results
  • Downloadable site database for offline and scripted checks
  • No account and no tracking of your searches
  • Dataset maintained and used by investigators worldwide
  • Free forever, open source (MIT)
osint.install_guide:
No installation needed: it runs in your browser.

  1. Open the WhatsMyName web app below.
  2. Type the username and press enter.
  3. Click any found result to open and verify the profile.
osint.use_case:
A stranger's DM offers you a part-time "rating task" job and asks you to move to another chat app. Before replying, paste their username into WhatsMyName. In thirty seconds you see whether the handle exists anywhere else: a years-old gaming profile suggests a real person, while zero hits anywhere suggests a handle invented for this scam.

Use the result to decide the next step. Real presence plus a verifiable history? Continue carefully. No presence at all? Block, report, and optionally escalate the handle to Sherlock for a deeper pass.
osint.faqs:
Do I need to install WhatsMyName?

No. It runs entirely as a web page — open it, type a username, read the results.

What does a hit prove?

That the username exists on that site. It does not identify the person behind it; that needs corroborating evidence.

Can I check several usernames at once?

The web UI checks one at a time. For batches, use the project's JSON list with a script, or a CLI tool such as Sherlock or Maigret.

Where does the site list come from?

A community-maintained JSON file in the project repository. Sites are added and corrected by pull request, so the list is current but not exhaustive.

osint.name: Censys
osint.summary: Search internet-facing hosts and TLS certificates by IP, organisation or domain, then monitor what changes. Freemium web app and API.
osint.overview:
Censys crawls the public internet and indexes hosts, services and certificates, so you can see what an organisation exposes without sending a single packet to it. Certificate search is the standout: certificates are public by design, and they map domains to organisations far more reliably than a WHOIS record.

Free accounts get host and certificate search with limited API credits; monitoring, historical scans and bulk exports are paid.
osint.key_features: Host and service search; TLS certificate index; organisation, ASN and IP pivots; change monitoring (paid); REST API.
osint.install_guide:
# Web search - no install
# https://search.censys.io

# API v2 with curl (create a free API key first)
export CENSYS_API_ID=your-id CENSYS_API_SECRET=your-secret

curl -s -u "$CENSYS_API_ID:$CENSYS_API_SECRET" \
  "https://search.censys.io/api/v2/hosts/search?q=example.com&per_page=25"

The free tier caps API credits and hides historical data; the web UI stays usable for ad-hoc checks. Docs: https://search.censys.io/api
osint.faqs:
Is Censys free?

There is a free tier: host and certificate search in the web UI, with a monthly API credit allowance. Monitoring, history and bulk exports need a paid plan.

How is it different from Shodan?

Shodan is built around banners and device fingerprints; Censys is built around certificates and host services. Certificate search makes Censys better for mapping an organisation's domains.

Does using it scan the target?

No. You are reading an index that Censys built with its own crawlers, so nothing is sent to the target while you search.

Why does a certificate show domains that no longer resolve?

Certificates outlive the hosts they were issued for. Historical certificates are often the only evidence left of a decommissioned service.
osint.use_case: You know one domain. Pivot through its certificates to find sibling hosts, staging environments and forgotten subdomains that no DNS list you can enumerate would show.

osint.name: Maltego
osint.summary: Graph people, domains, emails and organisations, then expand them with transforms that pull live data. Free Community Edition.
osint.overview:
Maltego models an investigation as a graph: every entity is a node, and every transform is a call to a data source that adds or links nodes. Instead of reading five tools' output in five tabs, you watch one graph grow and can see which facts actually connect.

The Community Edition is free for non-commercial use with a limited transform set; commercial and deep-web transforms are licensed.
osint.key_features: Entity graphs; transform library (DNS, WHOIS, social, breach); link analysis; export to CSV/GraphML; team sharing in paid tiers.
osint.install_guide:
# Desktop application - download from the vendor
# https://www.maltego.com/downloads/

# 1. Install, then register a free Community Edition licence in the app
# 2. New graph -> drag an Entity onto the canvas (Domain, Email, Person)
# 3. Right-click the entity -> Run Transform -> pick a source

# Useful first transforms on a Domain entity
#   DNS from DNS -> To DNS Name
#   To Website [Quick Lookup]
#   To Email addresses from Domain

Transforms need API keys for some sources; the free ones (DNS, WHOIS, quick lookups) work out of the box. Docs: https://docs.maltego.com/
osint.faqs:
Is Maltego free?

The Community Edition is free for non-commercial use with a limited transform set. Commercial use and the deeper data integrations are paid.

Maltego or a bunch of CLI tools?

CLI tools give you raw rows. Maltego's value is the graph: it keeps provenance for every edge, so you can show how two entities are connected instead of asserting it.

Do the transforms touch the target?

Some do: DNS and direct lookups contact third parties or the target itself. Others read existing datasets. Check each transform before running it on live scope.

Can I export the graph?

Yes - CSV, GraphML and image export on the free tier, which is enough to attach evidence to a report.
osint.use_case: Take an email address, expand it to its domain, the domain to its registrant and hosts, and the hosts to their certificates - then read the graph to see which of those links are real and which are coincidence.

osint.name: GHunt
osint.summary: Turn one Gmail address into the linked Google account: name, profile photo, YouTube channel and account identifiers. Free CLI.
osint.overview:
GHunt answers a narrow question very well: what does Google itself reveal about a Gmail address? It reads the public profile, the linked YouTube channel and the account metadata that Google's own pages expose, which is usually enough to attach a real name and photo to an address.

It authenticates with your own Google session cookies, so results come back at the same level a normal signed-in user would see.
osint.key_features: Gmail to Google account; public profile and photo; linked YouTube channel; account creation hints; JSON output for reports.
osint.install_guide:
# Isolated install
pipx install ghunt

# One-time login: follow the browser steps it prints and paste the cookies
ghunt login

# Look up an address
ghunt email target@gmail.com

# Machine-readable output for a report
ghunt email target@gmail.com --json out.json

Only look up accounts you have a legitimate reason to investigate. Docs: https://github.com/mxrch/GHunt
osint.faqs:
Is GHunt free?

Yes, it is free and open source. There is no key and no paid tier - it uses your own Google session.

Does the target get notified?

No. It reads public profile pages and Google's own account endpoints, which do not notify the account owner.

Why does login fail after a while?

The session cookies expire. Run ghunt login again and paste fresh values from a browser.

Does it work for non-Gmail addresses?

It reports whether the address has a Google account at all; the profile detail only exists when one does.
osint.use_case: Confirm whether an address is a real, active Google account before you spend a day pivoting on it - and get the profile name and photo that turn an email into a person of interest.

osint.name: Have I Been Pwned
osint.summary: Check whether an email appears in known data breaches, and read the full list of incidents it was caught in. Free web lookup.
osint.overview:
Have I Been Pwned is the reference breach index: an address is matched against hundreds of publicly disclosed breaches, and the result names each incident, the data classes involved and the date. It is the fastest way to tell whether an address has real exposure or only looks interesting.

The website is free. The API needs a paid key, with a free tier for a few well-known use cases (and a separate free Pwned Passwords range API).
osint.key_features: Breach lookup by email; per-breach data classes and dates; paste monitoring; domain search (paid); Pwned Passwords k-anonymity API.
osint.install_guide:
# Web lookup - no install
# https://haveibeenpwned.com

# Pwned Passwords API is free and needs no key (k-anonymity lookup)
curl -s https://api.pwnedpasswords.com/range/21BD1 | head

# Breach API needs a key from https://haveibeenpwned.com/API/Key
curl -s -H "hibp-api-key: $HIBP_KEY" \
  "https://haveibeenpwned.com/api/v3/breachedaccount/target@example.com"

The breach API answers 404 when an address is not in any breach - that is a clean result, not an error. Docs: https://haveibeenpwned.com/API/v3
osint.faqs:
Is it free?

The website is free. The breach API needs a paid key; the Pwned Passwords range API is free and needs no key at all.

Does checking an address notify its owner?

No. Lookups do not contact the account or notify anyone - but do not enter addresses you are not authorised to investigate into a third-party site.

HIBP says no breaches - is the address safe?

It means no incident in this index matched. Private breaches that were never disclosed will not appear anywhere.

Can I search a whole domain?

Domain search exists on the paid API and shows which addresses in a verified domain appear in breaches.
osint.use_case: Before you trust an address in a report, check what has already leaked from it. A breach hit tells you which passwords and identifiers are public, which changes how you describe the risk.

osint.name: dnstwist
osint.summary: Generate look-alike domains - typos, homoglyphs, bitsquatting and TLD swaps - and check which ones are already registered. Free, Python.
osint.overview:
dnstwist produces the domain permutations an attacker would buy: character swaps, omissions, additions, keyboard neighbours, homoglyphs and alternative TLDs. It then resolves them, so you can separate theory from domains that actually exist.

Point it at your own brand. The registered-and-resolving output is the shortlist for phishing monitoring and for takedown requests.
osint.key_features: Permutation fuzzing; homoglyph and bitsquatting sets; DNS resolution; WHOIS and MX lookup; optional screenshot capture; JSON/CSV output.
osint.install_guide:
# Python package
python3 -m pip install --user dnstwist

# or
pipx install dnstwist

# Every permutation, but only the ones that resolve
dnstwist --registered example.com

# Add MX records and a JSON report
dnstwist --registered --mxcheck --format json example.com > lookalikes.json

# Screenshot the registered look-alikes (needs a browser)
dnstwist --registered --screenshots example.com

Run it against your own domain, not a third party's. Docs: https://github.com/elceef/dnstwist
osint.faqs:
Is dnstwist free?

Yes - free and open source, maintained on GitHub. It runs entirely from your machine.

Why do so many permutations resolve?

Parked domains and wildcard DNS answer for almost anything. Filter on content or MX records before treating a hit as a threat.

Does it scan the look-alike sites?

Only optionally, with --screenshots. By default it resolves names and reads DNS and WHOIS records.

Can it cover a whole list of domains?

Feed it one domain per run, or loop it in a script - the JSON output is designed to be diffed between runs.
osint.use_case: Register a short watchlist: run dnstwist weekly against your brand, diff the registered list, and investigate anything new that resolves with a login page on it.

osint.name: Recon-ng
osint.summary: Metasploit-style console for OSINT: workspaces, modules and a database that keeps every finding queryable. Free, open source.
osint.overview:
Recon-ng puts reconnaissance in a console with workspaces, so an engagement's domains, hosts, contacts and credentials land in one database you can query instead of in a dozen text files. Modules are installed from its marketplace on demand, which keeps the default install small.

It is a framework, not a scanner: you choose the modules, and it stores what they return.
osint.key_features: Workspaces per investigation; module marketplace; SQLite-backed results; report generation; API-key management per module.
osint.install_guide:
# Isolated install (Python 3)
pipx install recon-ng

# Start the console and create a workspace
recon-ng
[recon-ng] > workspaces create example-investigation

# Install the modules you need, then run one
[recon-ng] > marketplace install hackertarget
[recon-ng] > modules load recon/domains-hosts/hackertarget
[recon-ng][example-investigation][hackertarget] > options set SOURCE example.com
[recon-ng][example-investigation][hackertarget] > run

# Everything it found is now in the database
[recon-ng] > show hosts

Some modules need API keys, set with keys add. Docs: https://github.com/lanmaster53/recon-ng
osint.faqs:
Is Recon-ng free?

Yes - free and open source. Individual modules may need their own free or paid API keys.

How is it different from theHarvester?

theHarvester gives you a report for one domain. Recon-ng gives you a database across a workspace, with modules you add as needed.

Where is my data stored?

In a local SQLite database inside the workspace directory - nothing is uploaded unless a module sends it to a third-party API.

Is the marketplace still maintained?

The core project and the marketplace both receive updates; check that a module still works before relying on it, since third-party APIs change.
osint.use_case: Run one organised pass over an in-scope domain: subdomains from several sources, then hosts, then contacts - all stored in a workspace you can export when the engagement ends.
