pentest.name: Aircrack-ng
pentest.summary: Wi-Fi security auditing for networks you own: capture handshakes and test encryption strength. Free.
pentest.overview:
Aircrack-ng is the standard suite for auditing Wi-Fi security on networks you own or are authorized to test. Capture a WPA handshake from your own access point, then test offline whether the passphrase resists dictionary attack — the honest way to answer if your wireless password is actually strong.

The suite covers the full workflow: put the card in monitor mode, discover networks, capture handshakes, crack or verify them, and audit WPS and enterprise setups. Practice entirely on your own lab router; radiating attacks at neighbors' networks is illegal in most places regardless of intent.
pentest.key_features:
• Full workflow: monitor, capture, crack, verify
  • WPA/WPA2 handshake capture and offline testing
  • WPS and enterprise assessment tools
  • Packet injection and replay utilities
  • Works with common USB adapters in monitor mode
  • Free and open source (GPL)
pentest.install_guide:
# Debian / Ubuntu / Kali (needs a monitor-mode capable adapter)

sudo apt install aircrack-ng



# Monitor mode on your lab adapter

sudo airmon-ng start wlan0



## Capture a handshake from YOUR access point

sudo airodump-ng --bssid AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF -c 6 -w lab wlan0mon



# Test the capture against a wordlist (offline, your own network)

aircrack-ng -w words.txt lab-01.cap
pentest.use_case: Your new office runs WPA2 with a short shared key taped to the wall. With approval, capture your own handshake in the lab and run it against a wordlist: it falls in minutes. The report justifies unique per-device credentials and a guest network before move-in day.
pentest.faqs:
Is Aircrack-ng free?

Yes. The whole suite is free and open source.

Do I need a special Wi-Fi adapter?

Yes. Monitor mode and packet injection need a chipset that supports it (Atheros AR9271 and Alfa adapters are the usual picks). A stock laptop card usually cannot capture handshakes.

Is aircrack-ng still maintained?

The suite gets occasional maintenance releases rather than active feature work. It remains the reference toolkit for WPA handshake capture and cracking.

Can it crack WPA3?

Not really. WPA3-SAE removes the offline handshake attack aircrack-ng relies on; only downgrade and transition-mode weaknesses are in reach, and those need different tooling.

pentest.name: Autopsy
pentest.summary: Graphical digital-forensics platform for disk images: timeline, keyword search, artifact review and reporting. Free, on Windows, macOS and Linux.
pentest.overview: Autopsy is a digital-forensics platform built on The Sleuth Kit. It helps investigators examine disk images, file systems and artifacts using a guided interface. Preserve chain of custody and use evidence copies rather than modifying original media.
pentest.key_features: Graphical case workflow; disk-image analysis; file and artifact review; extensible modules.
pentest.install_guide:
# Debian / Ubuntu / Kali (GUI package)
sudo apt install autopsy

# macOS / Windows
# Download the installer from https://www.autopsy.com/download/

# Launch the desktop app, then open the case UI it starts
autopsy
# -> http://localhost:9999/autopsy

# The Sleuth Kit command-line tools ship alongside it
fls -r -p evidence.dd

First run: File -> New Case, add the disk image, enable the ingest modules you need. Setup and module reference: https://sleuthkit.org/autopsy/docs/
pentest.use_case: Create a case from a lab disk image, document relevant artifacts and export findings while preserving the original evidence.
pentest.faqs:
Is Autopsy only for cybercrime investigations?

No. It is also used for incident response, internal investigations and forensic training.

Does Autopsy modify the evidence?

No. It reads the image and writes findings to its own case database, so the original file is untouched. Work from a verified copy and record its hash.

Which image formats can it open?

Raw dd, E01/Ex01 (via libewf), VHD/VHDX and AFF, plus live local disks if you point it at one. Attached images open read-only.

Is there a free version?

Autopsy is free and open source (Apache 2.0). The paid Autopsy edition is a separate commercial product for large lab deployments.

pentest.name: BloodHound Community Edition
pentest.summary: Map Active Directory privilege paths in a graph and see which group memberships actually reach Domain Admin. Free CE, runs as a Docker stack.
pentest.overview: BloodHound Community Edition helps defenders and authorized testers analyze relationships in Active Directory and supported identity environments to understand how permissions and group memberships can create risky paths. Collection and analysis must be approved, and exported identity data should be treated as sensitive.
pentest.key_features: Relationship graphing; path analysis; identity and privilege review; investigation queries.
pentest.install_guide:
# BloodHound CE ships as a Docker stack (Docker Engine + the compose plugin)
curl -L https://ghst.ly/getbhce -o docker-compose.yml
docker compose up -d

# The first-boot admin password is printed once in the logs - copy it now
docker compose logs 2>&1 | grep -i "initial password"

# UI: http://localhost:8080/ui   (user: admin)

Collect data with SharpHound on a Windows host you own (or BloodHound.py from the CE download page), then upload the ZIP in the UI. Docs: https://bloodhound.specterops.io/
pentest.use_case: Analyze a lab domain or approved directory snapshot to identify excessive privileges and prioritize least-privilege remediation.
pentest.faqs:
Does a displayed path guarantee compromise?

No. It indicates a relationship to validate against actual permissions and environmental controls.

Which collectors work with CE?

SharpHound (the bundled Windows collector) and BloodHound.py for Linux. Match the collector version to the server version or the upload is rejected.

Is CE different from BloodHound Legacy?

CE is the supported product: it bundles Neo4j and PostgreSQL behind a web UI. Legacy (the old desktop app with a separate Neo4j install) is end-of-life.

Why is my upload rejected?

Almost always a version mismatch between SharpHound and the server. Download SharpHound from the CE instance itself rather than an old copy.

pentest.name: Burp Suite
pentest.summary: The standard web app testing proxy: intercept, inspect and modify traffic for apps you are authorized to test. Freemium.
pentest.overview:
Burp Suite is the industry-standard platform for web application security testing. Route your browser through its proxy on an application you are authorized to assess and every request becomes inspectable, repeatable and modifiable: replay login flows, fuzz parameters with Intruder, and scan passively as you click through the app.

The free Community edition covers the proxy, Repeater and Intruder (throttled) — enough to learn real methodology. Burp Suite Professional adds the active scanner, full-speed Intruder and project files for client work. Learn on free, pay when client engagements demand the speed.
pentest.key_features:
• Intercepting proxy with full request/response editing
  • Repeater for manual request tweaking and replay
  • Intruder for fuzzing and parameter brute force
  • Passive scanning while you browse normally
  • Extender API with a large extension marketplace (BApp Store)
  • Professional tier adds active scanning and full-speed attacks
pentest.install_guide:
No install needed for first look — download the Community edition below for your OS.

  1. Install Burp Suite Community and launch it with a temporary project.
  2. Open its built-in browser and visit your authorized test app (for example OWASP Juice Shop running locally).
  3. Turn Intercept on, submit the login form, and study the raw request.
  4. Send it to Repeater (Ctrl+R) and modify one parameter at a time.
pentest.use_case: A client asks you to test their staging store before launch. Proxy your browser through Burp, log in, and click through checkout while Repeater collects interesting requests. Fuzz the discount-code parameter with Intruder (throttled Community rate is fine for one field), find that stacked codes apply twice, and report it with the exact replayed request as proof.
pentest.faqs:
Is Burp Suite free?

Burp Suite Community is free. Burp Suite Professional is paid and adds the active scanner, full-speed Intruder and collaboration features.

Community vs Professional - what is missing?

Community has no active scanner, throttles Intruder and lacks the BApp API extensions. For learning, the proxy, Repeater and Decoder are all there.

Does it need Java?

Modern releases bundle their own runtime. If you use the standalone JAR instead, install a current JDK first.

Can I use it without a browser proxy setup?

Yes - the built-in browser is preconfigured. For your own browser, install the PortSwigger CA certificate, otherwise HTTPS sites fail to load.

pentest.name: dnsx
pentest.summary: Resolve and inspect DNS records at scale in a pipeline: A/AAAA/CNAME lookups, wildcard filtering and custom resolvers. Free, open source, Go.
pentest.overview: dnsx is a DNS toolkit from ProjectDiscovery that supports resolving hostnames and querying record types in reconnaissance pipelines. It can help validate candidate subdomains and enrich an asset inventory with DNS information.
pentest.key_features: DNS resolution; record-type queries; list input; machine-readable output.
pentest.install_guide:
# Go tool - put the Go bin directory on your PATH first
go install -v github.com/projectdiscovery/dnsx/cmd/dnsx@latest
export PATH="$PATH:$(go env GOPATH)/bin"

# Docker alternative
docker run --rm projectdiscovery/dnsx:latest -h

# Resolve A records and show the response
echo example.com | dnsx -a -resp

# Chain it: subdomains -> only the ones that actually resolve
subfinder -d example.com -silent | dnsx -silent -a -resp

-wd drops wildcard DNS answers, which otherwise look like thousands of real subdomains. Docs: https://docs.projectdiscovery.io/tools/dnsx/overview
pentest.use_case: Resolve a reviewed list of in-scope subdomains and record which names map to addresses before service discovery.
pentest.faqs:
Does DNS resolution prove a service is vulnerable?

No. It only provides DNS evidence; assess services separately.

How is it different from dig?

dnsx takes a list on stdin and returns one line per host, which makes it pipeline-friendly. dig answers one query at a time for humans.

Why do some hosts return nothing?

No A/AAAA record, or the resolver timed out. Raise -retry and -t, and use -wd to drop wildcard answers that would otherwise look like hits.

Does it resolve through my own resolver?

Yes - pass -r resolvers.txt to use a specific list, which is how you spot resolver-based split-horizon differences.

pentest.name: ffuf
pentest.summary: High-speed web fuzzer for directories, parameters, virtual hosts and headers. Free, open source, one binary that runs on any OS.
pentest.overview: ffuf is a fast web fuzzer used for content discovery, virtual-host discovery and parameter testing. It is flexible and powerful, so rate limits, wordlists and scope should be configured deliberately to avoid overwhelming services.
pentest.key_features: Content and path discovery; virtual-host fuzzing; parameter fuzzing; filters and matchers; prebuilt releases.
pentest.install_guide:
# Go (current release, no package lag)
go install github.com/ffuf/ffuf/v2@latest

# or
brew install ffuf
sudo apt install ffuf

# Directory discovery on a host you are authorized to test
ffuf -u https://lab.example.com/FUZZ -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/common.txt -mc 200,204,301,302,403

# Hide the noisy catch-all response by size
ffuf -u https://lab.example.com/FUZZ -w list.txt -fs 4242

# Fuzz a parameter value instead of a path
ffuf -u "https://lab.example.com/search?q=FUZZ" -w payloads.txt -mc all

FUZZ marks the injection point; -mc keeps only the status codes you care about. Docs: https://github.com/ffuf/ffuf
pentest.use_case: Use a small wordlist against a local lab or approved staging host to identify unlinked routes, then manually assess discovered endpoints.
pentest.faqs:
Is ffuf a vulnerability scanner by itself?

It finds responses worth investigating; response differences still need interpretation and verification.

Why am I getting thousands of 200s?

The target returns a catch-all page. Filter by size (-fs), word count (-fw) or line count (-fl) using the size of a known random path.

Can it fuzz more than paths?

Yes: FUZZ works in headers, POST bodies, host names and query values. Multiple wordlists in one run are supported with -w name:file and FUZZNAME placeholders.

How do I slow it down?

Lower -t (threads) and add -p 0.1-1.0 to delay between requests. Rate-limit yourself before someone else does.

pentest.name: Frida
pentest.summary: Dynamic instrumentation toolkit: hook functions, dump keys and trace calls in running mobile and desktop apps. Free, open source.
pentest.overview: Frida is a dynamic instrumentation toolkit that lets researchers observe and interact with running processes. It is widely used for application debugging, mobile security research and controlled runtime analysis. Use it only on apps and devices you own or are authorized to test.
pentest.key_features: Runtime instrumentation; scripting; multiple operating systems; language bindings; mobile and desktop workflows.
pentest.install_guide:
# Python client plus the CLI tools
python3 -m pip install --user frida-tools

# or
brew install frida

# List apps and processes on a USB-connected device
frida-ps -U

# Attach to an app and load your script
frida -U -f com.example.app -l hook.js

# Android: push frida-server for the matching architecture and run it as root
adb push frida-server /data/local/tmp/
adb shell "su -c /data/local/tmp/frida-server &"

Use only on apps and devices you own or have written permission to test. Docs: https://frida.re/docs/installation/
pentest.use_case: Use Frida in a test device to observe how your own app handles a sensitive function or stores data during a controlled test.
pentest.faqs:
Is Frida an automated vulnerability scanner?

No. It is an instrumentation framework that supports manual analysis and custom tooling.

Do I need a rooted device?

On Android, frida-server needs root unless you repackage the APK with the gadget. On iOS you need a jailbroken or otherwise instrumentable device.

What is the gadget?

A shared library you embed in an app so Frida can attach without a rooted device. Standard route for instrumenting your own production builds.

Python client or CLI?

Same engine. frida-trace and frida-ps are the quick CLI entry points; the Python API is what you use to automate a workflow.

pentest.name: Gitleaks
pentest.summary: Scan git history or a plain directory for committed API keys, tokens and passwords, then block new ones before the commit. Free, open source.
pentest.overview: Gitleaks scans repository content and history for patterns that resemble credentials, tokens and other secrets. A detection is a prompt to verify exposure and rotate any real secret immediately; removing a secret from the latest commit alone may not remove it from history.
pentest.key_features: Git history scanning; configurable rules; local and CI use; machine-readable reports.
pentest.install_guide:
# Homebrew, a release binary, or Docker (distro packages lag behind)
brew install gitleaks
go install github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks/v8@latest

# Scan a repository's full commit history
gitleaks git /path/to/repo -v

# Scan a directory that is not a git repository
gitleaks dir ./src -v

# Write a JSON report you can attach to a ticket
gitleaks git . --report-format json --report-path gitleaks.json

Since 8.19 the old gitleaks detect command is deprecated: use gitleaks git or gitleaks dir. Add --redact to keep the secret values out of CI logs. Docs: https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks
pentest.use_case: Add Gitleaks to your own project’s pre-commit or CI workflow to catch accidental secret commits before release.
pentest.faqs:
Does deleting a leaked token fix the incident?

Not by itself. Revoke or rotate the credential, investigate use and then clean repository history if appropriate.

Does it need the full git history?

No - gitleaks dir scans a plain directory. Full history catches secrets that were committed and later removed, which is exactly what leaks usually are.

How do I stop false positives?

Add an allowlist to .gitleaks.toml (path, regex or commit) or an inline 'gitleaks:allow' comment. Keep the baseline file for known, accepted findings.

Can it run before the commit?

Yes: gitleaks git --pre-commit --staged, wired through pre-commit or a git hook, blocks a secret before it ever reaches history.

pentest.name: Hashcat
pentest.summary: The fastest password recovery and auditing tool: measure hash-cracking resistance on your own hashes. Free, open source.
pentest.overview:
Hashcat is the reference password recovery tool, using your GPU to test billions of candidate passwords per second against hashes you own — audit dumps, forgotten archives, or test accounts. Security teams use it to answer one question honestly: how long would our users' passwords survive?

It supports hundreds of hash modes, rule-based mutations, mask attacks and combinator strategies that mirror real attacker tradecraft. The workflow is always the same: extract hashes from systems you administer, crack them in your lab, and turn every cracked password into policy — longer minimums, breached-password screening and multi-factor authentication.
pentest.key_features:
• Hundreds of hash modes: NTLM, bcrypt, WPA, Kerberos and more
  • GPU acceleration across NVIDIA, AMD and Intel
  • Dictionary, mask, combinator and rule-based strategies
  • Distributed cracking and session restore
  • Brain and markov-chain optimizations
  • Free and open source (MIT)
pentest.install_guide:
# Debian / Ubuntu (needs OpenCL/CUDA drivers for GPU)

sudo apt install hashcat



# Dictionary attack on your own NTLM dump

 hashcat -m 1000 hashes.txt rockyou.txt



## Show already-cracked results

 hashcat -m 1000 hashes.txt rockyou.txt --show



## Mask attack: 8-char lowercase + digits

hashcat -m 1000 hashes.txt -a 3 ?l?l?l?l?l?l?l?l?d
pentest.use_case: After a policy review, extract the NTLM hashes from your own test domain controller into an isolated lab machine. Run a dictionary plus rule attack: 30% fall in an hour. That number — not an opinion — justifies the new 14-character minimum and breached-password blocklist in Monday's proposal.
pentest.faqs:
Is Hashcat free?

Yes. It is free and open source.

Which hash modes do I need?

Mode IDs select the algorithm: 0 MD5, 1000 NTLM, 1400 SHA-256, 22000 WPA. Run hashcat -h once and keep the mode list handy.

Why does it say 'no hashes loaded'?

The hash file format is wrong for the chosen -m, or the file has extra whitespace. Check with --identify first.

GPU or CPU?

GPU is the point - hashcat drops to a fraction of its speed on CPU. If OpenCL cannot see your GPU, fix the driver before blaming the tool.

pentest.name: httpx
pentest.summary: Turn a host list into live HTTP services: status codes, titles, TLS details, headers and detected tech in one fast pass. Free, Go CLI.
pentest.overview: ProjectDiscovery httpx is a command-line HTTP toolkit for probing web services and collecting response metadata. It helps turn candidate hostnames into a more useful list of live HTTP(S) endpoints for an authorized assessment.
pentest.key_features: HTTP/HTTPS probing; status and title collection; technology and response metadata; stdin and JSON workflows.
pentest.install_guide:
# ProjectDiscovery httpx - not the Python httpx library, which also ships an `httpx`
go install -v github.com/projectdiscovery/httpx/cmd/httpx@latest
export PATH="$PATH:$(go env GOPATH)/bin"

# Probe one host for status code, title and detected tech
httpx -u https://lab.example.com -status-code -title -tech-detect

# Turn a subdomain list into the live HTTP services
subfinder -d example.com -silent | httpx -silent -mc 200,302

# Show response headers and CDN/WAF fingerprints
httpx -u https://lab.example.com -headers -cdn

If pip install httpx is already on the machine, call the Go binary by full path to avoid hitting the Python one. Docs: https://docs.projectdiscovery.io/tools/httpx/overview
pentest.use_case: After passive subdomain discovery, probe the in-scope host list to identify which services respond over HTTP or HTTPS.
pentest.faqs:
Is this the Python httpx library?

No. This entry is ProjectDiscovery’s security reconnaissance CLI.

What does it actually check?

Whether a host speaks HTTP(S), then status code, title, TLS details, response headers, detected technologies and CDN/WAF fingerprints.

Why do some hosts time out?

Port 443/80 may be filtered, or the service is not HTTP. Add -ports and -timeout, and remember no response is itself a finding.

Can it screenshot pages?

Not by itself. Chain katana or gau for URLs and use a headless browser for screenshots - httpx stays a fast metadata prober.

pentest.name: Hydra
pentest.summary: Online login auditing against your own services: test credential strength where you are authorized. Free.
pentest.overview:
THC-Hydra tests online logins — SSH, FTP, web forms, databases — against password lists, on services you own or are explicitly authorized to assess. Where Hashcat cracks stolen hashes offline, Hydra knocks on the front door, which makes it the right tool for answering: would a password-guessing attack against our login actually succeed?

It is loud by design: every attempt is a real login, so rate-limit it, warn your defenders, and prefer it against staging. Pair every cracked credential with the same remediation — lockout policy, MFA, and breached-password screening at registration.
pentest.key_features:
• Dozens of protocols: SSH, FTP, HTTP(S), SMB, databases
  • Parallel tasks with tunable aggression
  • Username and password list combinators
  • HTTP form brute force with success/failure matching
  • Resume files for long assessments
  • Free and open source (AGPL)
pentest.install_guide:
# Debian / Ubuntu / Kali

sudo apt install hydra



## Audit SSH on your lab host (4 parallel tasks)

hydra -l admin -P words.txt -t 4 ssh://192.168.1.10



## Audit a web login form on your staging app

 hydra -l user@example.com -P words.txt 192.168.1.20 http-post-form "/login:email=^USER^&pass=^PASS^:Invalid credentials"
pentest.use_case: Your staging environment mirrors production logins. With approval, run Hydra with a small known-bad list against the staging SSH: two service accounts fall immediately. Those accounts get rotated, MFA-enforced, and added to the deploy checklist so production never ships them.
pentest.faqs:
Is Hydra free?

Yes. It is free and open source.

Why do I keep getting 'target refused'?

Wrong service module or port. Point -s at the real port and confirm the protocol with nmap first; hydra guesses the module, it does not detect it.

Is account lockout a risk?

Always. Hydra will happily lock every account on a real system. On authorized tests set -t low, -W between attempts, and agree a lockout threshold with the owner.

SSH keeps failing - why?

Modern OpenSSH limits auth attempts per connection (MaxAuthTries). Use -t 4 and expect slow progress; brute forcing SSH is usually the wrong approach.

pentest.name: Impacket
pentest.summary: Python implementations of SMB, MSRPC, Kerberos and LDAP with ready scripts such as secretsdump and psexec. Free, open source.
pentest.overview: Impacket is a collection of Python classes and tools for working with network protocols. Security teams use it for protocol analysis, interoperability testing and authorized Windows-domain assessments; some utilities are highly intrusive, so use a dedicated lab or an explicitly scoped engagement.
pentest.key_features: Protocol implementations; reusable Python libraries; example utilities; SMB and Windows-network workflows.
pentest.install_guide:
# Python library plus the example scripts (psexec.py, secretsdump.py, ...)
python3 -m pip install --user impacket

# isolated alternative
pipx install impacket

# Kali / Debian package
sudo apt install python3-impacket

# Dump NTLM hashes from an authorized lab host
impacket-secretsdump -just-dc-ntlm domain.local/user:'Password'@10.0.0.5

# Or run the scripts straight from a source checkout
python3 examples/psexec.py domain.local/user:'Password'@10.0.0.5

There is no impacket command on its own - every protocol is a separate script. Docs: https://github.com/fortra/impacket
pentest.use_case: In an isolated Windows lab, validate protocol behavior and document the minimum evidence needed for an authorized assessment.
pentest.faqs:
Is Impacket a single scanner?

No. It is a library and a collection of protocol-oriented tools.

Which scripts do I start with?

secretsdump.py for credential extraction, psexec.py, wmiexec.py and smbexec.py for execution, GetUserSPNs.py for Kerberoasting. Everything else builds on those.

Does it work from Linux against Windows?

Yes - that is its main use. It speaks the protocols natively over Python, so no Windows tooling is needed on the attacking side.

Is it maintained?

Actively, by Fortra (formerly SecureAuth). Install from PyPI rather than a stale distro package.

pentest.name: JADX
pentest.summary: Decompile Android APKs and DEX files into readable Java-like source, with a CLI and a GUI for following the code. Free, open source.
pentest.overview: JADX is a decompiler for Android DEX and APK files. It helps analysts navigate application code, inspect resources and understand implementation details, but decompiled output may be incomplete or misleading when obfuscation is present.
pentest.key_features: DEX/APK decompilation; GUI and CLI; resource decoding; code navigation and search.
pentest.install_guide:
# Kali / Debian
sudo apt install jadx

# macOS
brew install jadx

# Any OS: grab the release ZIP from https://github.com/skylot/jadx/releases

# Decompile an APK to readable Java sources
jadx -d out/ app.apk

# Open the GUI instead
jadx-gui app.apk

--no-res skips resources when you only want the code, and --deobf renames obfuscated classes to something readable. Docs: https://github.com/skylot/jadx
pentest.use_case: Inspect your own APK for hard-coded endpoints, insecure logic and exposed configuration, then confirm findings against runtime behavior.
pentest.faqs:
Is decompiled code identical to the original source?

No. Names and structure may be lost through compilation, optimization or obfuscation.

What if the app is obfuscated?

Run with --deobf to rename classes to readable placeholders, then follow the manifest and string constants. Obfuscation slows reading, it does not hide behaviour.

APK or DEX?

Both. An APK unpacks automatically; a bare classes.dex works too. Split APKs can be merged first with apkeep or a similar tool.

Why do some decompiled files fail?

Some methods defeat the decompiler and stay as smali. Read the smali, or try --show-bad-code to see what jadx produced.

pentest.name: John the Ripper
pentest.summary: Classic password auditing suite, best at slow hashes and encrypted files you own. Free, open source.
pentest.overview:
John the Ripper is the veteran password auditor, strongest where Hashcat is weakest: slow salted hashes, encrypted archives, documents and SSH keys you own and need assessed. Its "single crack" mode builds candidates from the account names themselves — exactly how lazy passwords are really chosen — and its wordlist-plus-rules engine squeezes maximum signal from minimum effort.

Use John for encrypted files and CPU-friendly audits, Hashcat when you have GPUs and fast hashes. Together they cover essentially every password audit a defender will ever run on their own systems.
pentest.key_features:
• Superb slow-hash and encrypted-file support
  • Single-crack mode from account metadata
  • Huge format library: archives, docs, keys, databases
  • Custom rules and incremental modes
  • Jumbo build adds community formats and MPI
  • Free and open source (GPL)
pentest.install_guide:
# Debian / Ubuntu / Kali

sudo apt install john



## Audit your own shadow-style file

john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt.gz hashes.txt



# Show cracked passwords

john --show hashes.txt



# Crack an encrypted zip you own (convert first)

zip2john protected.zip > zip.hash

john --wordlist=words.txt zip.hash
pentest.use_case: A departing contractor returns a laptop with an encrypted archive nobody can open. With written approval, convert it with zip2john and run a wordlist-plus-rules pass in your lab. The archive opens on a seasonal password — which becomes exhibit A for the new generated-password policy.
pentest.faqs:
John or Hashcat?

John for encrypted files and slow hashes on CPU; Hashcat for fast hashes on GPU. Auditors keep both.

Jumbo or core?

Take jumbo: it is the community build with GPU support, more formats and all the rules. Core is the minimal official tarball.

Where do I get wordlists?

rockyou.txt ships with Kali; SecLists is the larger general collection. Rules (best64, OneRuleToRuleThemAll) get more out of the same list than a bigger one.

How do I see cracked passwords?

john --show hashes.txt prints recovered ones, and --pot=name.pot keeps several engagements separate.

pentest.name: Katana
pentest.summary: Crawl web applications for URLs and endpoints, parsing JavaScript and known files so you see the routes a user can really reach. Free, Go CLI.
pentest.overview: Katana is a configurable web crawler from ProjectDiscovery. It supports standard and headless crawling modes and can help map routes, links and endpoints that should be reviewed during an application security assessment.
pentest.key_features: Web crawling; JavaScript-aware options; scope controls; JSON output; pipeline support.
pentest.install_guide:
# Go
go install github.com/projectdiscovery/katana/cmd/katana@latest
export PATH="$PATH:$(go env GOPATH)/bin"

# Crawl a target three levels deep, parsing JavaScript for endpoints
katana -u https://lab.example.com -d 3 -jc

# Store every URL found for later testing
katana -u https://lab.example.com -d 2 -silent -o urls.txt

# Feed a list of hosts instead of one URL
katana -list hosts.txt -silent -d 2

-jc parses JavaScript and -kf all keeps known files such as robots.txt and sitemap.xml. Docs: https://docs.projectdiscovery.io/tools/katana/overview
pentest.use_case: Crawl a staging application within an approved scope to build a route inventory for manual review and controlled testing.
pentest.faqs:
Should every discovered URL be tested automatically?

No. Review scope and avoid state-changing or destructive requests without approval.

Crawling or parsing?

Both in one pass: standard mode follows links found in HTML, -jc also extracts endpoints from inline and external JavaScript.

Why so few results?

The site may be JS-rendered. Add -headless to run a real browser, which is slower but sees what a user sees.

Does it respect scope?

Only what you give it. Use -fs to filter out off-domain URLs so you do not wander outside the engagement scope.

pentest.name: Kiterunner
pentest.summary: API route brute forcing that matches full REST path shapes and methods, not just directory names. Free, open source, prebuilt binaries.
pentest.overview: Kiterunner is an API discovery tool designed to identify routes and endpoints that conventional web content lists may miss. Use it in a controlled environment with explicit authorization, conservative request rates and an approved target list.
pentest.key_features: API-focused route discovery; route wordlists; CLI workflow; useful alongside proxy-based manual testing.
pentest.install_guide:
# Prebuilt binary from the releases page
# https://github.com/assetnote/kiterunner/releases
# The archive already contains the wordlists/ directory
tar -xzf kiterunner_*_linux_amd64.tar.gz
sudo mv kr /usr/local/bin/

# Or build from source
git clone https://github.com/assetnote/kiterunner.git
cd kiterunner && make build && sudo cp dist/kr /usr/local/bin/

# API route brute force with the bundled kite wordlist
kr scan https://lab.example.com -w routes.kite -x 20 -j 100

kr brute does plain directory brute forcing; kr scan matches wordlist routes against real API endpoints. Docs: https://github.com/assetnote/kiterunner
pentest.use_case: Test an owned staging API to find undocumented routes, then verify access controls manually using test accounts.
pentest.faqs:
Does discovering a route confirm an API vulnerability?

No. It identifies endpoints to inspect for authentication, authorization and input-validation issues.

Why not just ffuf?

Kiterunner matches full REST route shapes (path plus method plus expected response size), so it finds API endpoints that word-for-word directory brute force misses.

Do I need Assetnote wordlists?

The release bundles routes.kite, which is enough to start. The Assetnote API wordlists add coverage if you register for them.

What do the flags mean?

-x is concurrency, -j is the number of requests per second to hold back, and --ignore-length drops the wildcard response size.

pentest.name: Masscan
pentest.summary: The fastest internet-scale port scanner: sweep entire ranges in minutes on your authorized targets. Free, open source.
pentest.overview:
Masscan is built for one job — scanning very large networks very fast. Where Nmap carefully fingerprints each host, Masscan blasts SYN packets asynchronously and can cover the entire public IPv4 space in minutes from a fast connection. Authorized teams use it to inventory their own external footprint: every exposed port across every IP they own, refreshed regularly.

Speed has a price: Masscan fingerprints less per host than Nmap, so the standard workflow is Masscan to find what answers, then Nmap to examine the interesting hosts closely. Never point it at ranges you do not own — internet-wide scanning without authorization will get your address blocklisted and possibly your account suspended.
pentest.key_features:
• Internet-scale speed: millions of packets per second
  • Async stateless design with minimal memory use
  • Banner grabbing for service identification
  • Output compatible with Nmap XML tooling
  • Configurable transmit rate to stay inside policy
  • Free and open source (AGPL)
pentest.install_guide:
# Build from source (Ubuntu/Debian)

sudo apt install git gcc make libpcap-dev

 git clone https://github.com/robertdavidgraham/masscan.git

cd masscan && make



## Scan your own /24 for web ports (set YOUR rate)

sudo ./bin/masscan 203.0.113.0/24 -p80,443 --rate=1000



## Banner grab on the hits

sudo ./bin/masscan 203.0.113.0/24 -p80,443 --rate=1000 --banners
pentest.use_case: Your company owns a /24 it has not audited in years. With written authorization, run Masscan across it for common ports at a modest rate. Every unexpected open port — a forgotten camera, a dev database, a printer admin page — goes into the remediation queue, and the full sweep takes minutes instead of the weekend Nmap would need.
pentest.faqs:
Masscan or Nmap?

Masscan finds what answers across huge ranges fast; Nmap examines each host deeply. Use Masscan for discovery, Nmap for detail.

Why does 65536 packets per second matter?

Masscan is asynchronous and stateless: it sends and forgets, which is why it can scan the whole IPv4 space quickly and why it needs raw socket privileges.

Is it legal to scan the internet?

Scanning hosts you do not own is not authorized testing. Restrict --exclude / -iL lists to your own ranges, and never point it at a third party.

How do I get one line per open port?

-oL out.txt gives a grep-friendly list, --rate controls speed, and --source-ip sets the interface address when you have several.

pentest.name: Metasploit
pentest.summary: Modular exploitation framework: search by CVE, pick the target and payload, open a session. Free Framework; Pro adds automation and reporting.
pentest.overview:
The Metasploit Framework is the world's most used penetration testing platform: thousands of vetted exploit, auxiliary, payload and post-exploitation modules behind one consistent console. In authorized engagements it turns a confirmed vulnerability into demonstrated impact — a shell, a screenshot, a dumped hash proving the finding is real rather than theoretical.

The Framework itself is free and open source; Metasploit Pro adds automation, reporting and team workflows for professional shops. Learn the Framework in an isolated lab (Metasploitable is built for exactly this), earn the methodology, and only ever point modules at targets inside your written scope.
pentest.key_features:
• Thousands of vetted exploit and auxiliary modules
  • Meterpreter post-exploitation payloads
  • Consistent console, database and reporting workflow
  • Payload generation (msfvenom) for authorized testing
  • Lab-ready targets like Metasploitable and OWASP projects
  • Framework free and open source; Pro adds team automation
pentest.install_guide:
# Kali Linux (preinstalled) — or install Omnibus nightly

curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rapid7/metasploit-omnibus/master/config/templates/metasploit-framework-wrappers/msfupdate.erb > msfinstall && chmod 755 msfinstall && ./msfinstall



# Console against your LAB target only

msfconsole



## Example flow (Metasploitable lab)

use exploit/unix/ftp/vsftpd_234_backdoor

set RHOSTS 192.168.1.20

check

run
pentest.use_case: In your isolated lab, boot Metasploitable and confirm the vsftpd backdoor with check before running anything. The resulting shell lets you demonstrate, step by step, how an unpatched 2011 service becomes full compromise — the exact narrative that turns a vulnerability scan printout into a budget for patching.
pentest.faqs:
Is Metasploit free?

The Framework is free and open source. Metasploit Pro (automation, reporting, team features) is paid.

Framework or msfconsole?

The package is Metasploit Framework; the console you actually use is msfconsole. Start there, run 'search ' and read the module options.

Community or Pro?

Framework (Community) is free and includes the exploit modules. Pro adds automation and reporting for professional engagements.

Why does an exploit just fail?

Target mismatch, wrong payload or a patched service. Check the module's targets and set RHOSTS/LHOST/LPORT correctly before assuming the exploit is wrong.

pentest.name: Mobile Security Framework (MobSF)
pentest.summary: Static and dynamic analysis for Android APK/AAB and iOS IPA: permissions, secrets, network config and runtime behaviour. Free, runs in Docker.
pentest.overview: MobSF is an automated mobile application security assessment framework for inspecting application packages and, in supported environments, observing runtime behavior. It helps teams review permissions, insecure configuration, embedded secrets and other mobile-app risk indicators.
pentest.key_features: Static analysis; supported dynamic analysis workflows; report generation; Android and iOS assessment support.
pentest.install_guide:
# Docker is the supported install for the whole framework
docker pull opensecurity/mobile-security-framework-mobsf:latest
docker run -it --rm -p 8000:8000 opensecurity/mobile-security-framework-mobsf:latest

# UI: http://127.0.0.1:8000   (first login: mobsf / mobsf - change it)

# REST API instead of the UI
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/v1/upload \
  -H "Authorization: YOUR_API_KEY" -F "file=@app.apk"

The REST API key is shown at the bottom of the MobSF home page. Analysis runs locally - the APK never leaves your machine. Docs: https://mobsf.github.io/docs/
pentest.use_case: Analyze an application build you own or have permission to assess, then verify each important finding against the source or runtime behavior.
pentest.faqs:
Can MobSF guarantee an app is secure?

No. Automated results need manual review and platform-specific testing.

Does my APK leave my machine?

No. MobSF runs locally in Docker and stores reports in a local volume; nothing is uploaded to a third party by default.

What can it analyse?

Android APK/AAB, iOS IPA and source archives. Static analysis is immediate; dynamic analysis needs a rooted Android emulator connected to the container.

Is the API usable in CI?

Yes - upload via /api/v1/upload, scan via /api/v1/scan and pull the JSON report. That is the usual way to gate a mobile build.

pentest.name: Nikto
pentest.summary: Fast web-server vulnerability scanner: outdated software, misconfigurations and dangerous files on your hosts. Free.
pentest.overview:
Nikto scans web servers for thousands of known issues: outdated versions with CVEs, default files, misconfigurations and potentially dangerous endpoints. Point it at your own hosts and within minutes you hold a prioritized list of what to patch, remove or restrict.

It is deliberately noisy and fast rather than subtle — a first-pass hygiene check, not a stealth tool. Run it against every public web server you own on a schedule; pair anything it flags with manual verification, since version-based findings need confirming against your actual build.
pentest.key_features:
• Thousands of checks for CVEs, defaults and misconfigurations
  • Reports with CVE references and remediation hints
  • HTML, XML and CSV output for ticketing
  • SSL, authentication and proxy support
  • Tuning flags to match your stack and cut noise
  • Free and open source (GPL)
pentest.install_guide:
# Debian / Ubuntu / Kali

sudo apt install nikto



## Basic scan of your own host

nikto -h https://staging.example.com



## Save HTML report for the ticket

nikto -h https://staging.example.com -o nikto-report.html



## Tune out false positives for your stack

nikto -h https://staging.example.com -Tuning 1234567890abc
pentest.use_case: Before a release, run Nikto against your staging server. It flags an outdated admin panel and a directory listing you forgot. Both become pre-release tickets, verified fixed with a re-scan — two findings that never reach production.
pentest.faqs:
Is Nikto free?

Yes. It is free and open source.

Is a Nikto result a vulnerability?

No. It is an indicator: a header version or a file that looks interesting. Confirm manually before it goes in a report.

Why is it so slow?

Nikto runs over 6,000 checks with evasion and timing tunables. Use -Tuning to cut the check set and -maxtime to bound the run.

Does it handle HTTPS and auth?

Yes: -ssl, and -id user:pass for HTTP basic auth. For modern apps it is a supplement to a proxy-based scanner, not a replacement.

pentest.name: Nmap
pentest.summary: The standard network scanner: discover hosts, ports and services on networks you are authorized to test. Free, open source.
pentest.overview:
Nmap (Network Mapper) is the reference tool for network discovery and security auditing. Point it at a host or range you own or are authorized to assess and it reports which hosts are up, which ports are open, what services answer, and — with OS detection — what is likely running underneath. Almost every authorized assessment starts here, because you cannot secure what you have not mapped.

Defenders run it on their own infrastructure to find forgotten exposures before attackers do: the unpatched camera, the database port answering the whole internet, the test server nobody took down. Every probe Nmap sends goes to a target you named, so keep scans inside your authorized scope and rate-limit wide ranges.
pentest.key_features:
• Host discovery, port scanning and service version detection
  • OS fingerprinting and traceroute mapping
  • NSE scripting engine with hundreds of audit scripts
  • Output in XML, JSON-friendly and grepable formats
  • Stealth, timing and decoy options for authorized evasion testing
  • Free and open source — the industry baseline scanner
pentest.install_guide:
# Debian / Ubuntu / Kali

sudo apt install nmap



## macOS

brew install nmap



# Fast ping sweep of your lab subnet

nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24



# Service and version detection on one host

nmap -sV 192.168.1.10



# OS detection plus default scripts (slower, noisier)

sudo nmap -A 192.168.1.10
pentest.use_case: A client authorizes a black-box review of their office network. Start with a ping sweep of the provided lab range to list live hosts, then run service detection on each one. The resulting host-port-service inventory becomes the scope map for everything that follows — and any host answering that is not on the client's asset list becomes finding number one.
pentest.faqs:
Is Nmap free?

Yes. Nmap is free and open source.

Which script category should I start with?

default (-sC) for safe discovery, then vuln or discovery scoped to the ports you found. Never run vuln against hosts you do not own.

Why does the scan say 'filtered'?

A firewall is dropping the probes. Try -Pn to skip host discovery and a slower -T2 timing profile before concluding the host is down.

Is -A too noisy?

-A turns on OS detection, version detection, scripts and traceroute at once. On a real engagement use the individual flags so you know what caused each alert.

pentest.name: Nuclei
pentest.summary: Template-driven scanner for CVEs, misconfigurations and exposed panels across thousands of community checks. Free, open source, Go.
pentest.overview: Nuclei is a configurable vulnerability scanner from ProjectDiscovery that uses templates to check for known exposures and security conditions. Results require triage and confirmation; templates and target scope should be reviewed before running scans.
pentest.key_features: Template-based checks; severity filtering; JSONL output; custom templates; CI-friendly execution.
pentest.install_guide:
# Go
go install -v github.com/projectdiscovery/nuclei/v3/cmd/nuclei@latest

# or Docker
docker run --rm projectdiscovery/nuclei:latest -h

# Templates are a separate download - fetch them first
nuclei -update-templates

# Scan one authorized target with CVE and misconfiguration templates
nuclei -u https://lab.example.com -tags cve,misconfig

# Only high and critical findings, saved to a file
nuclei -u https://lab.example.com -severity high,critical -o findings.txt

-rl caps requests per second; keep it low on production-like labs. Docs: https://docs.projectdiscovery.io/tools/nuclei/overview
pentest.use_case: Run an approved, reviewed template set against staging assets, then manually validate high-impact findings before opening remediation tickets.
pentest.faqs:
Does a Nuclei alert always mean a confirmed vulnerability?

No. Verify the response and affected version or behavior before reporting.

Where do templates come from?

The nuclei-templates repository, pulled with -update-templates. Pin a version in CI so a template change does not silently alter results.

Can I write my own?

Yes - a YAML file with a request and matchers. Custom templates are how teams cover business logic that the public set does not know about.

Why do I get so many results?

Rate and scope. Use -severity, -tags and -rl to keep the run focused, and treat every hit as a lead to verify.

pentest.name: OWASP Amass
pentest.summary: Map an organisation's external attack surface with passive DNS, certificate and WHOIS correlation. Free, open source, an OWASP project.
pentest.overview: OWASP Amass helps security teams map domains, subdomains and related assets through OSINT and network-mapping techniques. Use it to build an evidence-based inventory of assets that belong to an organization before an authorized assessment.
pentest.key_features: Asset discovery; DNS and domain intelligence; attack-surface mapping; structured asset data.
pentest.install_guide:
# Build from source (upstream install path)
go install -v github.com/owasp-amass/amass/v4/...@master
export PATH="$PATH:$(go env GOPATH)/bin"

# Kali / Debian
sudo apt install amass

# Passive subdomain enumeration
amass enum -d example.com

# Add brute forcing and zone walking (slow and noisy - labs only)
amass enum -active -d example.com -brute -w wordlist.txt

Results are written to a database by default; -o subs.txt also prints them, and -df selects a different store. Docs: https://owasp.org/www-project-amass/
pentest.use_case: A security team uses Amass to compare the approved asset inventory with externally discoverable hosts and investigate unexpected exposure.
pentest.faqs:
Is Amass free?

The project is open source. Use it only for domains and assets you are authorized to assess.

Why is it so slow?

Amass correlates dozens of passive sources and builds a graph. First runs are minutes; the -timeout and -max-dns-queries flags bound it.

What is the database for?

Enumeration results land in a local graph database so later queries and the visualisation can reuse them. -df points it at another store.

Active or passive?

Passive sources only query third parties. -active and -brute send traffic to the target, so they need explicit authorization.

pentest.name: OWASP ZAP
pentest.summary: Free, open-source web app scanner and proxy from OWASP. Automate baseline scans of your own apps. Free forever.
pentest.overview:
OWASP ZAP (Zed Attack Proxy) is the free, community flagship for web application testing. Like Burp it proxies your browser traffic for manual inspection, and unlike Burp Community it ships a full active scanner, spider, fuzzer and a powerful REST API for CI pipelines — free forever, maintained by OWASP contributors and sponsors.

Teams wire ZAP into deployment pipelines so every release of their own app gets an automated baseline scan: spider the app, run the active scan against staging, fail the build on high-severity alerts. Beginners start with the automated scan button; professionals drive everything through the API.
pentest.key_features:
• Intercepting proxy plus full active vulnerability scanner
  • Traditional and AJAX spiders for coverage
  • Fuzzer, forced browse and custom scan policies
  • REST API and automation framework for CI pipelines
  • Add-on marketplace with community scan rules
  • Free and open source forever (OWASP flagship)
pentest.install_guide:
No install needed for first look — download ZAP below for your OS.

  1. Launch ZAP and run the Automated Scan against your local test app (OWASP Juice Shop on localhost).
  2. Read the Alerts tree: red and orange items first.
  3. Open one alert, read its description and solution, and verify it manually in the proxied browser.
  4. Re-scan after fixing to confirm the alert clears.
pentest.use_case: Your team ships a new customer portal every sprint. Add a ZAP baseline scan to the staging pipeline: spider, active scan, export the alert report. When the sprint adds a forgotten debug endpoint, ZAP flags it before release — the fix lands the same day instead of becoming an incident.
pentest.faqs:
Is ZAP really free?

Yes — every feature, including the active scanner and API, is free and open source.

Is ZAP a replacement for Burp?

It is a credible free alternative: proxy, spider, passive and active scanning, plus automation via the packaged scans in the API. Burp wins on extensions and manual workflow.

How do I scan an authenticated app?

Record a login in the AJAX spider with a context, then reuse that context for the active scan. Unauthenticated scans miss most of the app.

Can it run in CI?

Yes - zap-baseline.py and zap-full-scan.py in Docker are the standard approach, and the Automation Framework is the current recommended route.

pentest.name: Prowler
pentest.summary: Audit AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes and Microsoft 365 against hundreds of security checks with read-only access. Free, open source.
pentest.overview: Prowler is a cloud security assessment tool that checks supported cloud environments against security best practices and frameworks. It can help identify risky configurations and produce evidence for remediation, provided access is scoped appropriately.
pentest.key_features: Cloud posture checks; supported cloud providers; report outputs; CI and scheduled assessment workflows.
pentest.install_guide:
# Isolated install (recommended - Prowler pins many SDK versions)
pipx install prowler

# or
python3 -m pip install --user prowler

# Docker
docker run --rm -ti toniblyx/prowler aws

# Assess a cloud account with a read-only profile
prowler aws --profile lab-readonly

# Save machine-readable reports next to the console output
prowler aws -M csv json html -o ./reports

Azure, GCP, Kubernetes and M365 use their own subcommands (prowler azure, prowler gcp, prowler kubernetes). Docs: https://docs.prowler.com/
pentest.use_case: Run a read-focused assessment against your own cloud account and prioritize public exposure, identity and logging findings.
pentest.faqs:
Does Prowler need cloud credentials?

Many assessments require permissions to read configuration. Use least-privilege, review the official guide and protect generated reports.

What permissions does it need?

Read-only: SecurityAudit plus ViewOnlyAccess covers most checks. Prowler never changes your account, but it does call many read APIs.

Who pays for the API calls?

You do - checks are metadata calls, which are free in AWS, but a cross-account run still needs credentials for every account.

How do I track a fix?

Export to CSV/JSON/OCSF and diff two runs. The delta is your progress; a single report is only a snapshot.

pentest.name: Schemathesis
pentest.summary: Property-based fuzzing for OpenAPI, Swagger and GraphQL APIs: it generates hostile inputs from your own spec. Free, Python CLI.
pentest.overview: Schemathesis generates property-based API tests from an API schema and explores edge cases that ordinary example-based tests may miss. It is useful for finding contract violations and unexpected server behavior in APIs you own or are authorized to test.
pentest.key_features: Schema-driven test generation; OpenAPI and GraphQL support; reproducible cases; CI integration.
pentest.install_guide:
# Python package - the CLI is `st` (with `schemathesis` as an alias)
python3 -m pip install --user schemathesis

# or
pipx install schemathesis

# Fuzz a live API using its OpenAPI document
st run https://lab.example.com/openapi.json --checks all

# Local schema file against a local server
st run ./openapi.yaml --url http://127.0.0.1:8000

# CI-friendly: cap examples and return non-zero on failures
st run https://lab.example.com/openapi.json --max-examples 50

--stateful=links chains requests (create then read then delete) to catch sequence bugs. Docs: https://schemathesis.readthedocs.io/
pentest.use_case: Run schema-based tests against a local or staging API and investigate reproducible failures before release.
pentest.faqs:
Does Schemathesis replace manual API security testing?

No. It complements authorization, business-logic and abuse-case testing.

What does it find that unit tests miss?

Inputs nobody thought of: negative numbers in IDs, huge strings, wrong content types, and 500s raised where the spec promised 400.

Does it need a running server?

Yes - it talks to the live API, or to a WSGI/ASGI app through the Python integration for in-process testing.

Can I use it with any framework?

Anything that publishes OpenAPI, Swagger 2.0 or GraphQL. The spec is the contract; Schemathesis attacks that contract.

pentest.name: Semgrep
pentest.summary: Static analysis that understands code structure, so it catches tainted input and risky patterns without a build step. Free, open source.
pentest.overview: Semgrep scans source code for patterns that may indicate security bugs, unsafe APIs and policy violations. It supports developer workflows and CI checks, but findings must be reviewed in context to distinguish exploitable issues from false positives.
pentest.key_features: Static analysis; customizable rules; multi-language support; CI integration; community rule collections.
pentest.install_guide:
# Python package
python3 -m pip install --user semgrep

# or
brew install semgrep

# Docker
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/src" semgrep/semgrep semgrep scan --config auto

# Scan the current repository with the community rules
semgrep --config auto .

# Use a published ruleset and fail CI on findings
semgrep --config p/owasp-top-ten --error ./src

--config auto picks rules from the languages it detects; pin a ruleset instead for reproducible CI runs. Docs: https://semgrep.dev/docs/
pentest.use_case: Scan a repository you maintain before merging a change, then fix confirmed high-impact issues and add regression tests.
pentest.faqs:
Can static analysis prove exploitability?

No. Use the finding as a lead and validate data flow, reachability and impact.

Is it just regex?

No - it parses the code into an AST, so a rule matches structure and data flow, not text. That is why it survives reformatting and catches tainted input.

How fast is it?

Seconds on a mid-sized repo for a small rule set, which is why it works as a pre-commit or PR gate rather than a nightly job.

Which rules do I start with?

--config auto picks community rules from the detected languages. Pin a ruleset (p/owasp-top-ten, p/secrets) for reproducible CI results.

pentest.name: SpiderFoot
pentest.summary: Automate OSINT collection across 200+ modules from one web UI or CLI, with a correlator that links findings into a graph. Free and open source.
pentest.overview: SpiderFoot automates open-source intelligence collection and links findings across supported modules. It is useful for broad reconnaissance, but collected data should be validated and handled with privacy and scope considerations.
pentest.key_features: Modular OSINT collection; web UI; multiple source modules; exportable findings.
pentest.install_guide:
# From source (Python 3)
git clone https://github.com/smicallef/spiderfoot.git
cd spiderfoot
python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python3 sf.py -l 127.0.0.1:5001

# Docker
docker run -p 5001:5001 smicallef/spiderfoot

# UI: http://127.0.0.1:5001

Start with a domain or IP in "New Scan", pick the modules you want, then read the graph. Most passive modules need no API key; a few improve with one. Docs: https://www.spiderfoot.net/documentation/
pentest.use_case: Use a carefully scoped scan to organize public information about your own domain and identify items that need manual validation.
pentest.faqs:
Is SpiderFoot fully passive?

Behavior depends on enabled modules and data sources; review module behavior before a run.

How many modules does it have?

Over 200, split into passive (third-party data) and active (direct to target) sets. Passive modules need no API key; the key-based ones add depth.

What is the correlator for?

It cross-links findings from different modules, which is how a domain turns into an organisation, then into contacts. Without it, you just get rows.

Can I run a scan from the CLI?

Yes: sf.py -s example.com -t DOMAIN_NAME -m all -o tab. Useful for scheduled recon; the UI is for exploring results.

pentest.name: SQLMap
pentest.summary: Automatic SQL injection detection and exploitation testing for your own apps and labs. Free, open source.
pentest.overview:
SQLMap automates the tedious part of SQL injection testing: give it a URL, request file or Burp log from an application you are authorized to assess and it detects injectable parameters, fingerprints the database, and — with explicit flags — enumerates tables or dumps data to prove impact.

Its real value is coverage and rigor. Manual testing finds the easy cases; SQLMap systematically tries boolean, time-based, error-based and stacked-query techniques across every parameter, including ones buried in cookies and headers. Use it to confirm findings on your test apps, and always stay inside authorized scope — dumping data you should not see is the line between testing and crime.
pentest.key_features:
• Automatic detection across boolean, time, error and stacked techniques
  • Database fingerprinting: type, version, user and privileges
  • Table enumeration and controlled data dumping for proof
  • Tests URLs, forms, cookies, headers and JSON bodies
  • Accepts Burp request files directly (-r)
  • Free and open source (GPL)
pentest.install_guide:
# Debian / Ubuntu / Kali

sudo apt install sqlmap



## Test a parameter on your lab app

sqlmap -u "http://localhost:3000/product?id=1" --batch



## Fingerprint the database once injection is confirmed

sqlmap -u "http://localhost:3000/product?id=1" --banner --current-db



# Capture a Burp request to a file, then test it

sqlmap -r login-request.txt --batch
pentest.use_case: While testing your staging store in Burp you notice the product filter reflects input oddly. Save the request to a file and run SQLMap against it: it confirms a time-based injection in ten minutes. Fingerprint the database, document the exact payload and remediation (parameterized queries), and stop there — the proof is complete without touching customer data.
pentest.faqs:
Is SQLMap free?

Yes. It is free and open source.

Which level and risk should I use?

Start at --level=1 --risk=1. Raising them multiplies requests and, at risk 3, adds payloads that can damage data - only on labs.

How do I avoid breaking the app?

--batch for unattended runs, --threads 1-2, and a scope you own. Test only parameters you are authorized to test.

It says 'not injectable' - am I done?

No. Try --level=5 --risk=2 with the right technique (--technique=BEUSTQ), or the parameter may need a cookie or header injection point.

pentest.name: Subfinder
pentest.summary: Passive subdomain enumeration from 30+ public sources, ready to pipe straight into httpx or nuclei. Free, open source, Go.
pentest.overview: Subfinder is a passive subdomain-enumeration tool from ProjectDiscovery. It aggregates results from supported public sources and is designed to fit into repeatable reconnaissance workflows without making active probes the default.
pentest.key_features: Passive subdomain discovery; configurable data sources; JSON output; pipeline-friendly CLI.
pentest.install_guide:
# Go
go install -v github.com/projectdiscovery/subfinder/v2/cmd/subfinder@latest
export PATH="$PATH:$(go env GOPATH)/bin"

# Docker
docker run --rm projectdiscovery/subfinder:latest -d example.com

# Passive subdomains only, one per line
subfinder -d example.com -silent

# Use every source and save the result
subfinder -d example.com -all -o example-subs.txt

# Feed straight into httpx to find live web services
subfinder -d example.com -silent | httpx -silent

Optional API keys go in ~/.config/subfinder/provider-config.yaml and add sources that need them. Docs: https://docs.projectdiscovery.io/tools/subfinder/overview
pentest.use_case: Use Subfinder to discover known public subdomains for a domain in scope, then validate and prioritize the results before testing.
pentest.faqs:
Does Subfinder need API keys?

Some data sources require provider keys. Check the official installation guide for current requirements.

Passive only - is that enough?

It finds names that already appear somewhere public: certificates, DNS datasets, search indexes. Names that were never published need brute forcing, which is a different tool.

How do I add API keys?

Put them in ~/.config/subfinder/provider-config.yaml. Sources without keys still work; keys mostly unlock more coverage and speed.

Why is a subdomain missing?

No single source sees everything. Add -all, add keys, and accept that passive enumeration is a starting list, not an inventory.

pentest.name: tcpdump
pentest.summary: Capture and filter network packets from the command line with pcap expressions, write a capture, then read it in Wireshark.
pentest.overview: tcpdump is a command-line packet analyzer used to capture and inspect traffic on supported network interfaces. It is lightweight and useful on servers where a graphical analyzer is unavailable; capture files can later be reviewed in Wireshark.
pentest.key_features: Command-line capture; Berkeley Packet Filter expressions; pcap output; remote-server troubleshooting.
pentest.install_guide:
# Debian / Ubuntu / Kali
sudo apt install tcpdump

# macOS ships an old build; Homebrew has a current one
brew install tcpdump

# Capture 20 packets on one interface, no DNS or port-name lookups
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -nn -c 20

# Filter by host and port, and write a pcap (-w writes files; there is no -o)
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -nn -w lab.pcap 'host 192.168.1.10 and tcp port 443'

# Read the capture back
tcpdump -nn -r lab.pcap

Capture only traffic on networks you own or administer. Filter syntax is pcap-filter(7), the same grammar Wireshark uses. Docs: https://www.tcpdump.org/manpages/tcpdump/
pentest.use_case: Capture a short, approved lab trace filtered to a specific host or port, then analyze the pcap locally.
pentest.faqs:
Does tcpdump decrypt TLS traffic automatically?

No. It can capture encrypted traffic, but decryption requires appropriate keys and supported conditions.

How do I capture on a busy link without dropping packets?

Write straight to disk with -w and increase the buffer with -B; analysis happens later in Wireshark. Printing decoded packets is what drops frames.

Why are my packets truncated?

Default snaplen cuts at 262144 bytes only if you set -s 0; otherwise set -s 0 explicitly to capture full frames.

Can I capture without root?

Yes if the binary has file capabilities (CAP_NET_RAW) or you belong to a group granted them. Distributions often ship both options.

pentest.name: testssl.sh
pentest.summary: Check TLS protocols, ciphers, certificates and known weaknesses on any host without sending data to a third party. Free, plain shell script.
pentest.overview: testssl.sh checks TLS-enabled services for protocol support, cipher configuration and selected cryptographic issues. It works from the command line and produces human-readable and machine-readable reports for remediation.
pentest.key_features: TLS protocol and cipher checks; machine-readable output; broad platform support; no separate package manager required for basic use.
pentest.install_guide:
# Plain shell script - nothing to compile
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/drwetter/testssl.sh.git
cd testssl.sh
./testssl.sh https://lab.example.com

# Docker
docker run --rm -it drwetter/testssl.sh https://lab.example.com

# Only the protocol and cipher sections
./testssl.sh --protocols --server-defaults https://lab.example.com

--fast skips the slow checks, --jsonfile out.json writes machine-readable output, and --color 0 keeps logs clean. Docs: https://testssl.sh/
pentest.use_case: Assess your own public-facing service or staging endpoint and use the report to prioritize outdated protocol and cipher settings.
pentest.faqs:
Can it test non-HTTPS services?

It supports TLS/STARTTLS services on various ports; check the official documentation for protocol-specific options.

What is the difference from an online SSL test?

Nothing is uploaded and nothing is stored: the script opens the same TLS connections from your machine, which is what you want for internal or pre-release hosts.

Why do some sections take minutes?

Several checks deliberately test slow or malformed handshakes. --fast skips them, and --wide adds even more.

Can I check a STARTTLS service?

Yes: --starttls smtp|imap|pop3|xmpp|ftp switches protocol, which is how you audit mail servers with the same script.

pentest.name: theHarvester
pentest.summary: Gather emails, subdomains, hosts and employee names for a domain from 20+ public sources. Free, open source, command line.
pentest.overview: theHarvester gathers publicly available information from supported sources to help map an organization’s external footprint. Results are leads to verify, not proof of ownership, exposure or vulnerability.
pentest.key_features: Public-source discovery; domain and email intelligence; exportable results; reconnaissance workflow support.
pentest.install_guide:
# Kali
sudo apt install theharvester

# pipx (keeps its pinned dependencies out of your system Python)
pipx install theHarvester

# From source
git clone https://github.com/laramies/theHarvester.git
cd theHarvester && pipenv install

# Sources that need no API key
theHarvester -d example.com -b crtsh,certspotter,otx,rapiddns -l 200

# Everything, into a report file
theHarvester -d example.com -b all -l 500 -f harvest.html

-d is the domain, -b the sources, -l the result limit and -f the output file. Docs: https://github.com/laramies/theHarvester
pentest.use_case: During an approved assessment, use public-source results to identify contact patterns and candidate subdomains for verification.
pentest.faqs:
Is every result accurate?

No. Sources may be incomplete or stale, so validate findings before reporting them.

Which sources need API keys?

crtsh, certspotter, otx, rapiddns and urlscan need none. Shodan, Hunter, SecurityTrails and similar read keys from api-keys.yaml.

Why does Google return nothing?

Google blocks automated queries quickly. Use bing, duckduckgo or crtsh instead, and keep -l modest.

Is this active scanning?

No - it queries third-party indexes and public sources. Nothing is sent to the target, which is why it is safe at the recon stage.

pentest.name: Trivy
pentest.summary: Find vulnerable dependencies, OS packages, IaC misconfigurations and secrets in images, repositories and clusters. Free, open source.
pentest.overview: Trivy is an open-source security scanner that can inspect container images, filesystems, repositories and supported configuration types for vulnerabilities and misconfigurations. It is useful for adding repeatable checks to development and deployment workflows.
pentest.key_features: Container and dependency vulnerability scanning; configuration checks; secret detection; CI integration.
pentest.install_guide:
# macOS / Linux Homebrew
brew install trivy

# Or the release binary from https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy/releases
# Debian/Ubuntu also have an official apt repository - see the docs link below

# Docker
docker run --rm aquasec/trivy image alpine:3.20

# Scan a container image
trivy image myapp:latest

# Scan a project directory for vulnerable dependencies and bad config
trivy fs .

# Infrastructure-as-code and secrets in one pass
trivy config . && trivy fs --scanners secret .

The vulnerability database is downloaded on first run and refreshed every 24 hours. Docs: https://trivy.dev/latest/docs/
pentest.use_case: Scan your own container image before publishing it and review high-severity results alongside base-image and dependency updates.
pentest.faqs:
Does a clean Trivy scan prove a container is secure?

No. Coverage depends on the scanned artifact, enabled checks and current vulnerability data.

What does it actually scan?

OS packages, language dependencies from lockfiles, container image layers, IaC manifests, Kubernetes manifests and (opted in) secrets.

Why a 24 hour database refresh?

It downloads the vulnerability DB on first run and caches it. In air-gapped CI, mirror the DB or pass --skip-db-update with a prebuilt cache.

Does it fail my build?

Only with --exit-code 1. Severity thresholds (--severity HIGH,CRITICAL) then define what counts as a failure.

pentest.name: TruffleHog
pentest.summary: Scan git history, filesystems and container images for secrets, then verify which keys are actually live. Free, open source.
pentest.overview: TruffleHog searches code and supported data sources for credentials and other secrets, with verification capabilities for supported detectors. Treat results as sensitive, restrict access to reports and rotate any confirmed credential promptly.
pentest.key_features: Secret discovery; supported source integrations; credential verification for supported detectors; CI use.
pentest.install_guide:
# Homebrew (Linux and macOS)
brew install trufflesecurity/trufflehog/trufflehog

# Docker
docker run --rm -it trufflesecurity/trufflehog:latest github --repo https://github.com/org/repo

# Scan a repository's full history and keep only live, verified secrets
trufflehog git https://github.com/org/repo --only-verified

# Scan a directory, or a container image
trufflehog filesystem ./path
trufflehog docker --image myapp:latest

--only-verified is the difference between a usable report and a wall of false positives - it calls the provider to test each key. Docs: https://github.com/trufflesecurity/trufflehog
pentest.use_case: Scan your own repositories and development history, verify findings safely, then revoke exposed credentials and prevent recurrence.
pentest.faqs:
Should scan results be published in tickets or public logs?

No. They can contain live credentials; redact them and restrict access.

What does verification mean?

It calls the provider with the discovered key. A live key is a real incident; an unverified string is a lead you still have to check.

Will it scan my whole organisation?

Per repository or per path. For org-wide coverage, run it in CI on every push and add the GitHub app or scheduled scans.

Does it handle non-git sources?

Yes: S3, GCS, Docker images, filesystem paths, Elasticsearch and more. Each has its own subcommand.

pentest.name: Volatility 3
pentest.summary: Memory forensics: extract processes, network connections and injected code from RAM captures. Free, open source, Python 3.
pentest.overview: Volatility 3 is an open-source memory-forensics framework for examining captured memory images. Analysts use plugins to investigate processes, modules and other artifacts, while preserving the original evidence and documenting acquisition context.
pentest.key_features: Plugin-based memory analysis; structured output; cross-platform Python tooling; incident-response workflows.
pentest.install_guide:
# Isolated Python install (recommended)
pipx install volatility3

# or
python3 -m pip install --user volatility3

# Identify the memory image before anything else
vol -f memory.raw windows.info

# Processes, network connections, loaded modules
vol -f memory.raw windows.pslist
vol -f memory.raw windows.netscan
vol -f memory.raw windows.dlllist

# Linux and macOS images use their own plugin namespace
vol -f memory.raw linux.pslist

Symbol tables (ISF) download on demand on first use - run once with network access. Docs: https://volatility3.readthedocs.io/
pentest.use_case: Analyze a memory image acquired from a system you administer, preserve the original file and document reproducible findings.
pentest.faqs:
Can memory analysis always identify malware?

No. Findings depend on image quality, operating-system support and available artifacts.

Where do the symbols come from?

Volatility 3 downloads ISF symbol packs on demand from the project's symbol server. Fetch them once in an environment with network access, then copy the cache.

Why does windows.info fail?

Almost always a missing or mismatched symbol pack, or an image that is not a raw memory capture. Check the file header first.

Can I use my own Linux kernel?

Yes, but you have to generate the symbol table (dwarf2json) from the matching kernel and put it in the symbols path.

pentest.name: Wireshark
pentest.summary: Deep packet analysis with the reference protocol dissector, plus tshark for scripted captures and filtering. Free, open source.
pentest.overview: Wireshark captures or opens packet traces and decodes protocols so analysts can investigate connections, troubleshoot networks and understand suspicious traffic. Capture only traffic you are authorized to monitor and protect sensitive packet files.
pentest.key_features: Protocol dissectors; display filters; packet stream inspection; capture and offline trace analysis.
pentest.install_guide:
# Debian / Ubuntu / Kali - installs the GUI, tshark and dumpcap
sudo apt install wireshark

# let your user capture without sudo, then log out and back in
sudo usermod -aG wireshark "$USER"

# macOS
brew install --cask wireshark

# Capture 10 packets from the command line
tshark -i eth0 -c 10

# Read a pcap and print the HTTP requests it contains
tshark -r lab.pcap -Y "http.request" -T fields -e http.host -e http.request.uri

-Y is the display filter language, -f is the capture filter. Get the filter right the first time in Wireshark's own reference. Docs: https://www.wireshark.org/docs/
pentest.use_case: Open a capture from your own lab and filter DNS, TCP or HTTP traffic to understand how an application communicates.
pentest.faqs:
Is Wireshark only for pentesting?

No. It is also widely used for network troubleshooting, incident response and protocol analysis.

Capture filter or display filter?

Capture filters (pcap syntax) decide what is recorded and cannot be changed later. Display filters (-Y) filter what you see and are the ones to use daily.

Why can I not see any interfaces?

Permissions. Add your user to the wireshark group (or use dumpcap with capabilities) and log back in.

How do I follow a TCP stream?

Right-click a packet and pick Follow -> TCP Stream in the GUI, or use -z follow,tcp,ascii,0 with tshark for the same output on the command line.
